newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel stocks end up as market awaits budget cuts.
newsitem.headline: Israel stocks end up as market awaits budget cuts.

text.p: Tel Aviv shares closed higher on Wednesday in thin trading as the market responded in a restrained fashion to the government's plan to make further cuts in the 1997 budget, traders said.
The benchmark Mishtanim index of the top 100 shares rose 0.56 percent, or 1.09 points, to 196.32 on a low all-share turnover of 62 million shekels against 60 million on Tuesday.
The Maof 25 blue chip index gained 0.63 percent to 206.03.
"Activity continues to be very low and it is difficult to buy or sell. This is not a real market," said Amir Eayal at Epsilon Securities.
Market players were divided as to whether approval by parliament of the proposed cuts would have an effect on shares.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the Treasury would propose an additional two billion shekels in 1997 budget cuts by early December. The additional spending reductions will come on top of 4.9 billion shekels in cuts the government has already submitted to parliament.
"Even if the government approves the budget cuts the market will remain stuck," said Eayal

But a trader at Bank Leumi said he thought the market would be watching budget developments. "Investors are now waiting to see what will happen with the budget cuts. It is still too early to predict what the government will do," he said.

"The Bank of Israel will have to lower the interest rates because all the indicators show that the economy is slowing. This will have a positive impact on the market. But, even then total volume will remain relatively low and it will be difficult to trade," Eayal added.
First International Bank of Israel surged 4.5 percent to 36,327 after it reported on Tuesday a third-quarter net profit of 54.2 million shekels against 33.3 million shekels a year earlier.
Blue Square Chain Stores Properties & Investments closed unchanged at 2,516 after it reported a third-quarter net profit of 15.39 million shekels against 12.99 million shekels a year earlier.
Agan Chemical Manufacturers rose 1.5 percent to 5,675 after Salomon Brothers raised its 1996 and 1997 earnings estimates for the company and maintained its buy recommendation.
Salomon boosted Agan's 1996 net income projection to $1.70 a share, versus $1.61 previous and $1.36 in 1995. Salomon said 1997 earnings would reach $1.83 a share, up from $1.78 a share previously.
The most active share was Super-Sol, which rose 0.75 percent to 7,868 on volume of 3.6 million shekels.

Bank Hapoalim, the second most active share, rose 0.75 percent to 464 on turnover of 3.1 million shekels after the Histadrut labour federation said it had signed an agreement to sell its three percent stake in the bank to a U.S. investor group for 168 million shekels.
Teva Pharmaceutical Industries, fell 2.5 percent to 145,069 on volume of 2.9 million shekels.
